items.title: Planes, Trains And Automobiles' Deleted Ending Was Rightfully Cut
items.summary: Planes, Trains and Automobiles was originally supposed to have a completely different ending, but thankfully it was removed before release. Few comedy movies have endings quite as emotionally satisfying as Planes, Trains and Automobiles. John Hughes' 1987 road-trip comedy spends most of its running time putting advertising executive Neal Page (Steve Martin) through an increasingly ridiculous series of travel disasters, largely thanks to his unwanted traveling companion, Del Griffith (John Candy). However, beneath the hilarious arguments, unfortunate misunderstandings and spectacular misfortunes is a surprisingly moving story about loneliness, friendship and the importance of appreciating other people.

items.title: Hexed review – Disney’s witchy caper is a wicked disappointment
items.summary:
A teen girl discovers she is a witch in this mostly magic-free reminder that original animation is stuck in an unoriginal place

As bleak as Disney’s overreliance on sequels might have become, it’s not quite as bleak as the crumbling state of its original output. Obviously because of the former, the latter category has become that much less populated but even when the studio has recently bothered to release something without a number in the title, it’s been hard to really see the point.

With or without Pixar, films like Elio, Strange World, Raya and the Last Dragon, Luca, Elemental, Onward and Wish have all felt as uninspired as something a rival might try to desperately cobble together in an attempt to lure kids away from Disney. Three Thanksgivings ago, Wish was a particularly poor yet extremely smug example of how rubbishy things have got, a personality-free princess tale that doubled up as a 100-year anniversary victory lap. It was Disney’s worst-reviewed animated film in almost two decades and its deserved box office failure cost about $131m. Unperturbed, its co-director Fawn Veerasunthorn (along with Moana 2 director Jason Hand) is back this holiday with another rote rip-off adventure that doesn’t deserve its place in the kingdom.

Continue reading...
items.t: Hexed review – Disney’s witchy caper is a wicked disappointment

items.title: Scream 4 came out 15 years ago – but its mockery of online brainrot is more spot-on than ever
items.summary:
When Wes Craven’s final slasher film came out, correctly predicting clout-chasing influencers and social media’s corruption of our lives, Instagram was just six months old

  • Get our weekend culture and lifestyle email

It has been almost a year since Australia’s social media ban for under-16s and it seems as though nothing has been able to effectively deter the youth from the slippery slope of internet addiction – even when they have expressed the desire to quit. It’s hard to believe that it has only been a decade since TikTok condemned us to the eternal doomscroll and just over 15 years since Instagram launched. Surely no one predicted just how much the online world would be leeching off of us, right? Well, Wes Craven did.

Craven is the mind behind notable horror titles including The Hills Have Eyes, A Nightmare on Elm Street and the Scream franchise – and the last film he directed, four years before his death in 2015, was Scream 4.

items.title: Robert Pattinson is not enough: who should become the new Bond girl?
items.summary:
With the British actor securing the role of James Bond, speculation has now begun over who should join him in Denis Villeneuve’s much-anticipated caper

After years of speculation, Robert Pattinson has been officially cast as James Bond for a new Amazon-produced film directed by Denis Villeneuve. There’s no release date for the project yet, though fall 2028 seems a likely target, given the release dates of all of the Pierce Brosnan and Daniel Craig installments. This leaves plenty of time left on the clock for more speculation – namely, about who will be cast as the so-called Bond Girls for this rebooted installment.

Past Bonds have usually been recognizable from earlier work, but none of them had yet reached Pattinson’s level of fame before actually playing Bond. Given that, in addition to sterling indie work for directors like David Cronenberg, Claire Denis and Lance Oppenheim, Pattinson has also been in Twilight, Batman and Christopher Nolan movies, he’s arguably already as famous as Brosnan and Craig were at their 007 peak. It must be this shift in the casting status quo that has inspired some predictions or hopes for a quantity as known as, say, Sydney Sweeney to play a Bond girl.

Continue reading...
items.t: Robert Pattinson is not enough: who should become the new Bond girl?

items.title: To Hold a Mountain review – a spectacular setting for tough savvy woman’s fight against the government
items.summary:
A livestock farmer with a sad secret in her past rallies to keep military training out of her breathtaking mountain home in Montenegro

An award-winner in Sundance, where it premiered earlier this year, this slow-burn documentary follows a middle-aged Montenegrin livestock farmer called Gara and her 13-year-old daughter Nada. The two of them eke out a hardscrabble living on Sinjajevina, a breathtaking mountain plateau on which Montenegro’s government would like to conduct training exercises for its own army as well as Nato’s. This goes down about as well as a wolf in the sheep pen with flinty Gara, who rallies her neighbours as well as the local media to fight the proposal. She displays a savviness that’s somewhat surprising, even if her fortitude and strength of conviction seem completely in character.

However, that fight against the state is just one element of a film that, through long, languid takes, reveals the women’s stately pastoral existence, one taken up above all with care for their menagerie of animals (cows, sheep, goats, cats and dogs) and each other. Co-directors Petar Glomazić and Biljana Tutorov gradually reveal the family setup isn’t exactly what it appears at first. Although Gara calls Nada her daughter, the young girl is actually her niece; Gara adopted her after her sister, Nada’s mum, was killed by a violent husband. Gara’s profound grief and loss haunt her every day, felt most painfully, perhaps, when an animal dies on the heath, reminding them of the fragility of life.
items.t: To Hold a Mountain review – a spectacular setting for tough savvy woman’s fight against the government

items.title: The World of Love review – beautifully directed and compellingly elusive family mystery
items.summary:
Yoon Ga-eun’s film tracks the uneasy fallout after a teenage schoolgirl makes a deeply shocking announcement to her class

Korean film-maker Yoon Ga-eun creates a strange world of bewilderment, sadness and pain – but not much of love – in this involving and mysterious family drama. It seems always to be gesturing at an indefinable sense of loss, a poignant keynote struck by the recurring soundtrack piano arrangement of Bach’s Sheep May Safely Graze.

Seo Su-bin gives an excellent performance as Joo-in, a high schooler possessed of a cheeky, madcap sense of fun, like her wacky, magic-obsessed kid brother Hae-in (Lee Jae-hee). She is keen on taekwondo and often shown (in borderline-uncomfortable closeup) kissing boyfriends that she will later dump. But when classmate Su-ho (Kim Jeong-sik) asks her to sign a petition objecting to the release and local rehousing of a convicted child rapist, Joo-in refuses, on the ostensible grounds that the petition talks about the permanent damage done to rape victims. Joo-in astonishes and upsets the class by announcing at the top of her voice that she herself is a rape victim, and she has not been permanently damaged – and then says it was just a joke.

Continue reading...
items.t: The World of Love review – beautifully directed and compellingly elusive family mystery

items.title: Everything Else Is Noise review – a musician attempts to raise her art above the cacophony of city noise
items.summary:
A TV shoot is beset with barking dogs, power cuts and personal animosities in Nicolás Pereda’s docufiction exploring the fight for artistic space in a world of distractions

This latest docufiction from Mexican-Canadian film-maker Nicolás Pereda finds rhythm amid chaos. The film opens with an amusing visual game of Tetris; at a busy intersection in Mexico City, the concept of designated lanes and traffic signals appears to be symbolic only. Here, driving is all about carving your own path, as crisscrossing cars squeeze their way past each other. Reminiscent of Jacques Tati’s ending to Playtime (1967), this entrancing dance of machines encapsulates Pereda’s central dilemma: the question of seizing one’s personal and artistic space amid a world of distractions.

The cacophony of honks and revving engines is accompanied by an expressionistic cello piece, played by a composer called Teresa (played by Teresita Sánchez). To some of her neighbours, however, her music is no different from the traffic noise. On this particular day, Teresa has opened her home to fellow musician Rosa (Rosa Estela Juárez Vargas), who wants to use the space for her interview with a two-man television crew. From a nearby dog’s loud barking to intermittent power cuts, the shoot is beset with continual interruptions; but the film also foregrounds the subtle frictions that grow between the characters. Panning shots swing from the banal questions posed by the male interviewers to the women’s unimpressed faces. We can sense that this is not the first time they have been faced with…

items.title: You Can See Everything passes $100m at global box office as UK release starts strong
items.summary:
The documentary from Nathan Fielder following fraudster Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks leading up to her imprisonment has broken box office records in the UK

Elizabeth Holmes film You Can See Everything has crossed the $100m mark at the global box office as it recorded the highest ever opening weekend figure for a non-music documentary in the UK.

Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, You Can See Everything earned an estimated $2.5m over the weekend on its sixth week of release in North America, according to Box Office Mojo, bringing its total there to $93.5m. This has been augmented by successful releases in a number of international territories, which has added an estimated $9m for a total of $102.5m.

items.title: You Can See Everything’s vibes-check approach is an insult to objective truth
items.summary:
For three hours, Nathan Fielder opts not to quiz convicted criminal Elizabeth Holmes on the details of her deception. Instead, he looks into her eyes and asks if she’s for real. Is that why his film has been so successful?

• This article does not contain major spoilers

Sometimes, people who have lied lie about whether or not they’ve lied. They even, on occasion, fail to tell the truth despite having sworn to do so – in court, for instance, or staring deeply into the eyes of someone who is sitting right there.

Is that a shock? Probably not. We all engage in versions of such behaviour every day. We understand that the current climate of mutually clueless echo chambers helps claptrap gain traction. But we can still recognise the difference between little white lies and big red flags. We know that the moment anyone starts using the phrase “my truth” it’s time to cancel the wedding.

Continue reading...
items.t: You Can See Everything’s vibes-check approach is an insult to objective truth

items.title: Delays mean Robert Pattinson doesn’t have to do a third Batman movie. DC Studios had better persuade him – and fast
items.summary:
The actor’s new role as James Bond could be bad news for DC, as a new owner, new chief and new director already threaten to shake and stir Gotham’s distinctive hero

Can one actor play both Batman and James Bond? This is the question many have been asking since Robert Pattinson was announced as the new 007. The obvious answer is yes: the 40-year-old Englishman has the poise, charisma and steel to join His Majesty’s Secret Service, and saving Gotham could soon become something he fits in between assignments.

Among all the furore over Pattinson’s appointment, it would have been easy to miss some rather less cheering news for the citizens of Gotham. According to the Wrap, delays to The Batman: Part II have freed the actor from his contractual obligation to make a third film. The sequel is now due in February 2028, almost six years after the first instalment. He could still sign a new deal, of course, but Warner Bros will have to persuade its caped crusader to stick around.

Continue reading...
items.t: Delays mean Robert Pattinson doesn’t have to do a third Batman movie. DC Studios had better persuade him – and fast
